background.definition: Lichen simplex chronicus is a localized eczematous plaque caused by repeated scratching and rubbing, which produces lichenification (thickening and accentuation of skin markings). Lesions may occur on normal skin or may result from an underlying pruritic condition. Prurigo nodularis is a closely related condition, likely simply a more severe manifestation.

list.listitem: Peak incidence is between 30 and 50 years of age.
LSC is more frequently diagnosed in women than in men.
Incidence is higher in patients with psychiatric comorbidity.
Nocturnal paroxysms of scratching may cause sleep disturbances, as demonstrated in polysomnographic studies.
Chronic pruritus may diminish quality of life.
Excoriated areas may become infected when colonized by Staphylococcus aureus.
Visible lesions may be aesthetically disturbing to the patient.
LSC may be caused by chronic scratching of normal skin or by localized and generalized pruritus (see ).
Psychiatric illness (anxiety or depression commonly) may exacerbate scratching, rubbing or skin manipulation.
LSC has been described in a patient with prolonged hyperphosphatemia.
Pruritus of known or unknown etiology leads to rubbing and scratching.
Nerve growth factor, substance P, various neuropeptides, mast cells, and eosinophils have been implicated in the inflammatory and pruritic response of skin in neurodermatitis.
Neuronal hyperplasia further sensitizes the skin to pruritus and increases the urge to itch in response to minor tactile, emotional, or environmental stimuli.
Habitual and unconscious scratching results in perpetuation of a vicious itch-scratch cycle that can be persist for months, years, or decades.
Suspect LSC in a patient presenting with a pruritic, well-demarcated, lichenified plaque at a site habitually scratched or rubbed. C
A potassium hydroxide (KOH) examination, fungal culture, or skin biopsy may help to rule out common mimics of LSC. C
Patch testing may help identify a contact etiology. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Hard papules at the back of the neck, often with hair emerging at the center
Onset around 2 years; family history of atopy, asthma, urticaria, hay fever; flexural creases in adults
Rash follows contact by hours; acutely vesicular in linear or geometric shape
Early stages resemble eczema but resist treatment; multiple biopsies may be required
Coin-shaped, vesicular at outset, intensely pruritic, resists treatment
Sharply demarcated plaques, silvery scale, nail pits, pinking of gluteal cleft
Skin scrapings reveal hyphae, responds to antifungals
Burrows, intensely pruritic, webspaces and genitalia affected, but scalp spared
Intensely pruritic, papulovesicular eruption, underlying gluten-sensitive enteropathy

list.listitem: Patients typically present with a lichenified plaque; history of pruritus or itching/rubbing varies. Early lesions are usually macular and erythematous. Plaques, lichenification, postinflammatory dyspigmentation (hypo- or hyperpigmentation), and scale appear later.

Itching may be more severe at bedtime, when patient is awake but inactive, and usually remits when patient is distracted. Areas accessible to scratching (e.g., neck, trunk, and extremities) are commonly affected; the middle of the back is usually spared.
Visible flexural eczema and onset before age 2 years suggest atopic dermatitis.
Comorbid anxiety disorders and depression may exist.
Diagnosis is usually clinical but in cases of uncertainty, consider performing diagnostic tests.

Perform KOH examination or fungal culture of skin scrapings (scale) to exclude tinea. Skin scrapings may be obtained by gently grazing a scalpel over the lesion and collecting scale on a microscope slide. Following the addition of a few drops of KOH 20% and gentle heating, light microscopy may reveal hyphae and spores.
Patch testing may be helpful if you suspect contact dermatitis.
When the diagnosis remains uncertain or the condition refractory to treatment, consider skin biopsy to establish the diagnosis of LSC and rule out other diagnoses.
The diagnosis is usually made on clinical grounds: lichenified plaque, pruritic, and a history of scratching/rubbing.
Rule out tinea with KOH test or fungal culture, and consider patch test if contact dermatitis is suspected.
Treat with topical corticosteroids and emollients. If the condition is refractory to treatment, consider biopsy.

Emollients are steroid sparing, help maintain treatment effects, and may prevent the formation of new plaques. A
Topical calcineurin inhibitors is favored in sensitive areas, such as the face, where long-term topical corticosteroid treatment may lead to atrophy or telangiectasias. B
Avoid scratching or rubbing. Stress reduction techniques and behavioral modification therapy may be useful. C
Oral antihistamines may help alleviate pruritus. C

Topical corticosteroids are the mainstay for the symptomatic treatment of LSC associated with atopic dermatitis or other pruritic dermatologic conditions. High-potency (class 1 or 2) corticosteroids are recommended for short courses on the scalp and volar surfaces. Low-potency (class 6 or 7) corticosteroids are generally appropriate for the face, axilla, and genitals. Mid-potency agents may be used elsewhere. To avoid atrophy and telangiectasias, the leading skin complications of long-term topical corticosteroid use, apply sparingly, use lower-potency corticosteroids where possible, and consider an intermittent schedule of application.
Topical alternatives to corticosteroids include topical calcineurin inhibitors (e.g., tacrolimus, pimecrolimus), doxepin, and aspirin in dichloromethane.

Tacrolimus (0.03% cream, 0.1% ointment) and pimecrolimus (1% cream) are effective for neurodermatitis or neurotic excoriations. Topical tacrolimus is favored for the face and genitalia as a steroid-sparing agent.

Doxepin 5% cream 4 times a day (without occlusive dressing) is effective for pruritus in patients with LSC, nummular eczema, or contact dermatitis; 60% had relief within 24 hours and 84% had relief after 7 days, significantly more than with vehicle cream.
Although not available in the United States, aspirin 3% in dichloromethane cream may be effective in patients who have not responded to topical corticosteroids.

A trial randomized 70 patients with prurigo nodularis to nemolizumab (an interleukin-31 receptor antagonist) or placebo. After 4 weeks, there was a 2.8 point greater reduction on a 10 point pruritus score, as well as a greater improvement in lesions.

A second trial randomized 274 adults with prurigo nodularis in a 2:1 fashion to nemolizumab or placebo. At 16 weeks, an itch response (defined as a 4+ point reduction on a 10 point scale) had occured more often with nemolizumab (56.3% vs 20.9%, p < 0.001, NNT = 4).

Another trial randomized 286 participants with moderate to severe prurigo nodularis to nemolizumab or placebo in a 2:1 ratio. At 24 weeks, itch response was greater with nemolizumab (58% vs 20%, p < 0.05, NNT = 3) as was the investigator's global assessment.
A longer term trial of nemolizumab found continued efficacy and minimal adverse effects at up to 68 weeks.
Hypnosis has been used successfully.
Medical resonance therapy music reduced scratching in patients with neurodermatitis.
Homeopathy is minimally, if at all effective, for the treatment of neurodermatitis.
Both electroacupuncture and auricular acupuncture have been shown to be effective in small studies.
Emollient use alleviates xerosis and associated pruritus.
Encourage patients to stop scratching. Cutting nails short and wearing mittens to bed may help. Patients should avoid wool, if they are sensitive.
Occlusive dressings may produce superior clinical results. However, they increase systemic absorption of corticosteroids and must be used judiciously when larger areas are involved.
Oral antihistamines, such as diphenhydramine or hydroxyzine, may alleviate pruritus.
Finely crushed ice may be applied to affected areas to reduce pruritus.
Employ stress reduction and behavioral modification therapy. Oral antidepressant or antianxiety agents may help some patients.
Consider a psychiatric referral if a mental health issue is suspected in the perpetuation of neurodermatitis.
Consider a dermatology referral for severe, recalcitrant cases, or when the diagnosis is in question.
LSC may improve with treatment, but scarring and postinflammatory dyspigmentation usually persist. C
Long-term maintenance treatment may be required. C
Exacerbation or recurrence is common at times of emotional stress. C
Mild-to-moderate topical corticosteroids along with emollients remain key therapies for pregnant women with LSC.
Topical corticosteroid use in pregnancy is controversial. However, with limited, intermittent, and localized use, the absorption rate is minimal and systemic side effects are rare.
There was no increased risk of teratogenicity with topical corticosteroids in 2 population-based studies.

Topical calcineurin inhibitors, such as tacrolimus or pimecrolimus, have limited bioavailability and there are no reported fetal anomalies. Systemic therapy, however, is teratogenic. Consequently, topical treatment may be considered only when optimal first-line therapies and safer second-line therapies have failed, and only if use is restricted to localized areas.
